turns.tutor:
A 4-bit free-running counter adds a fixed integer \(k\), where \(0 \le k \le 31\), once per clock, modulo 16. A logic analyzer records counter values \(3, 9, 15, 5\) on four consecutive rising edges.

What can you determine about \(k\) from these observations? Justify your answer.

turns.learner: Now show the checked key and a four-point partial-credit rubric. Can taking one more reading on the next clock distinguish all the candidates?
turns.tutor:
The samples determine **\(k \equiv 6 \pmod{16}\)**, so the candidates in \(0\le k\le31\) are **\(k=6\) and \(k=22\)**. There is no unique \(k\).

Each transition requires the same modular increment:
\[
9-3=6,\qquad 15-9=6,\qquad 5-15=-10\equiv6\pmod{16}.
\]
Both candidates reproduce every transition: adding \(22\) modulo \(16\) has exactly the same effect as adding \(6\). The range contains no other integers congruent to \(6\).

A proposed four-point rubric awards one point for each:

| Point | Requirement |
|---|---|
| 1 | Determines \(k\equiv6\pmod{16}\) from a transition. |
| 1 | Checks that this increment fits both remaining transitions, including the wraparound. |
| 1 | Identifies both \(6\) and \(22\) as candidates. |
| 1 | Justifies that these are all candidates in the stated range and concludes that \(k\) is not uniquely determined. |

**One more reading cannot distinguish them.** Both predict
\[
(5+k)\bmod16=11.
\]
Indeed, no number of further readings of this counter can distinguish them: for any current value \(x\),
\[
(x+22)\bmod16=(x+6)\bmod16.
\]
A next reading other than \(11\) would contradict the stated model rather than select a candidate.
